\chapter{Los Papeles Del Trabajo}
\label{ch:es-papeles}
\hlchaptermodality{435}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read a job advert, say what experience I have, and say what I must send and bring.}

Read the notice or advert this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el currículum]{el currículum — a word that stayed Latin}

\label{lesson:ES-C435-curriculum}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el trabajo}. Say \emph{el papel}. A job advert asks you to send one particular piece of paper. Name it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el currículum}
\textbf{el currículum} — the CV, the résumé.

The full form is \textbf{currículum vítae}, and in speech people usually say only \textbf{el currículum}, or shorten it further to \textbf{el currí}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{curriculum} meant \emph{a running}, a lap of a track — from \emph{currere}, to run. \emph{Currículum vítae} is \textbf{the running of a life}.

Spanish kept the Latin \textbf{-um} ending instead of reshaping it, which marks the word as a formal borrowing rather than an inherited one:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{inherited from Latin} & \textbf{borrowed from Latin} \\
\midrule
la puerta & el currículum \\
el agua & el álbum \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

An inherited word has been worn down by centuries of speech; a borrowed one was lifted from a book and still looks like it. That ending is the giveaway, and it tells you the register before you know the meaning: a word ending \textbf{-um} in Spanish is almost always formal, technical or administrative.

The same \emph{currere} is under \textbf{el curso} and \textbf{la carrera}, both of which are also runnings.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el currículum}
  \item send your CV
  \item what \emph{currículum vítae} means literally
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The CV? (\textbf{el currículum}.) What does the Latin mean? (\textbf{The running of a life}.) What does the \textbf{-um} ending tell you? (\textbf{It was borrowed, not inherited.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la documentación]{la documentación — the papers, as one thing}

\label{lesson:ES-C435-documentacion}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el currículum}. Say \emph{el papel}. The garage asked you to bring something more than one sheet. Name it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la documentación}
\textbf{la documentación} — the paperwork, the documents, your papers.

Singular in form and plural in meaning: one word for \textbf{the whole set}. \emph{Traiga la documentación} asks for all of it, not one sheet.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{documentar} plus \textbf{-ción}, the ending that turns an action into a thing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{the thing} \\
\midrule
documentar & la documentación \\
reparar & la reparación \\
informar & la información \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Fourth ending in five chapters, and the most productive of the lot. Almost any Spanish verb in \textbf{-ar} can take it, and English usually has the twin in \textbf{-tion} — so \textbf{-ción} words are the cheapest reading you will ever get.

One thing to watch: they are \textbf{always feminine}, whatever the verb, and the plural drops the accent — \emph{la reparación}, \emph{las reparaciones}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la documentación}
  \item bring the paperwork and your CV
  \item the noun made from \emph{reparar}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The paperwork? (\textbf{la documentación}.) What does \textbf{-ción} do? (\textbf{Turns an action into a thing}.) What gender are they? (\textbf{Feminine}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la experiencia]{la experiencia — the word you can already read}

\label{lesson:ES-C435-experiencia}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la documentación}. Say \emph{la empresa}. An advert wants one more thing from you before the papers. Say it and check your guess below.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la experiencia}
\textbf{la experiencia} — experience.

\textbf{experiencia previa} is the set phrase every job advert uses: \emph{se valora experiencia previa}, \emph{imprescindible experiencia previa}.

\begin{cousinweb}
You did not need this lesson to read the word, and that is worth noticing rather than passing over.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Spanish} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
la experiencia & experience \\
la diferencia & difference \\
la paciencia & patience \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{-encia} and English \textbf{-ence} are the same ending, inherited by both from Latin. Hundreds of words pair this way, and the pairing almost never misleads.

So the real content of this lesson is a \textbf{licence}: when a long Spanish noun ends in \textbf{-ción}, \textbf{-encia}, \textbf{-idad} or \textbf{-mente}, try the English twin first. You will be right far more often than wrong, and the cost of being wrong is a moment.

That is not true of short words, where the false friends live — \emph{embarazada} does not mean embarrassed, and \emph{éxito} is not exit. The long formal endings are the safe ones.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la experiencia}
  \item previous experience is essential
  \item two more words ending in \emph{-encia}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Experience? (\textbf{la experiencia}.) Which endings can you usually trust? (\textbf{-ción, -encia, -idad, -mente}.) Which words are risky? (\textbf{Short ones}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[previo]{previo — before this one}

\label{lesson:ES-C435-previo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{la experiencia}. The advert wants a particular kind of it — the kind you got somewhere else, earlier. Name that kind.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: previo}
\textbf{previo / previa} — previous, prior, earlier.

\textbf{experiencia previa} — previous experience. \textbf{sin previo aviso} — without prior warning, which is the other place you will meet it.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{pre-} before, plus \textbf{-vio} from \emph{via}, way. What lies on the way \textbf{before}.

The position is worth watching, because Spanish adjectives usually follow the noun and this one does both:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{phrase} & \textbf{where it sits} \\
\midrule
experiencia previa & after \\
sin previo aviso & before \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{Sin previo aviso} is a fixed phrase and keeps the older order. Fixed phrases preserve arrangements that ordinary speech has left behind, which is why they so often look like exceptions — they are the older rule, kept whole.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{previo}
  \item previous experience is essential
  \item without prior warning
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Previous? (\textbf{previo}.) Previous experience? (\textbf{experiencia previa}.) Without warning? (\textbf{sin previo aviso}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[jubilado]{jubilado — the participle that became a person}

\label{lesson:ES-C435-jubilado}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{el pedido}. Say \emph{el trabajo}. You learned that a participle can harden into a noun. Here it hardens into a \textbf{person}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: jubilado}
\textbf{jubilado / jubilada} — retired, and also \emph{a retired person}.

\textbf{jubilarse} — to retire. \emph{Se jubila en marzo} — she retires in March.

\begin{cousinweb}
Same move as \textbf{el pedido}, one chapter apart:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{verb} & \textbf{participle} & \textbf{used as} \\
\midrule
pedir & pedido & a thing \\
jubilar & jubilado & a person \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

A Spanish participle can stand as an adjective \emph{or} a noun with no further change, which is why \emph{un jubilado} needs no word for \emph{person} in it.

\textbf{And the root is not what you would expect.} Latin \emph{iubilare} meant to \textbf{shout for joy} — it is the same word under \emph{jubilee} and \emph{jubilant}. Retiring in Spanish is, etymologically, letting out a cheer.

Whether anybody feels that on the day is another matter, but the word was built by people who thought the end of work was worth shouting about.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{jubilado}
  \item a retired neighbour
  \item she retires in March
  \item the other participle-turned-noun you hold
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Retired? (\textbf{jubilado}.) To retire? (\textbf{jubilarse}.) What did the Latin root mean? (\textbf{To shout for joy}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(currículum, documentación …]{(currículum, documentación, experiencia, previo, jubilado) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R435-repaso-papeles}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{the CV}, \emph{the paperwork} and \emph{retired}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the endings that read themselves}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{ending} & \textbf{what it does} & \textbf{example} \\
\midrule
\textbf{-ción} & action becomes a thing & la documentación \\
\textbf{-encia} & pairs with English \emph{-ence} & la experiencia \\
participle & becomes a thing or a person & jubilado \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The participle row is the one to keep: \textbf{el pedido} in the first chapter of this run was a thing, \textbf{jubilado} here is a person, and neither needed an extra word to become one.

Five chapters have now handed you \textbf{-dor}, \textbf{-ería}, \textbf{-ero}, \textbf{-ción} and \textbf{-encia}. Do not read that as a rule that every word yields — \emph{el currículum} in this very chapter kept a Latin ending and yields nothing. The habit is to look, not to expect.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{You could say you had a job, and nothing about getting one.} \emph{El trabajo}, \emph{la empresa} and \emph{trabajar} were yours; the CV you send, the papers you bring, the experience an advert demands and the word for somebody who has stopped working were not.

A job advert is four lines long and uses all five. That is the shape of A2 reading: short, ordinary, administrative, and impossible without exactly these nouns.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item all five words
  \item previous experience is essential
  \item send your CV and bring the paperwork
  \item which one kept a Latin ending
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The CV? (\textbf{el currículum}.) Previous experience? (\textbf{experiencia previa}.) Retired? (\textbf{jubilado}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(un anuncio de trabajo) — four lines, five new words}

\label{lesson:ES-C435-sintesis-anuncio}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{experiencia previa}. The advert you are about to read turns on that phrase.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Read it once straight through, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{SE BUSCA DEPENDIENTE/A} Tienda del centro. Imprescindible \textbf{experiencia previa} de al menos un año. Enviar \textbf{currículum} y traer la \textbf{documentación} el día de la entrevista.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item how much experience they want
  \item what you have to send
  \item what you have to bring, and when
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Now produce it. Say aloud:

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item I have two years of previous experience
  \item I am sending my CV today
  \item my neighbour is retired and does not work now
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Five chapters, twenty-five words, and no new grammar at all.} Everything you said a moment ago uses tenses you held before this run started. What was missing was the vocabulary an ordinary week is made of — orders, buildings, machines, paperwork — and none of it appears in a beginner's dialogue, because beginners' dialogues are about holidays and hobbies.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you send? (\textbf{el currículum}.) What do you bring? (\textbf{la documentación}.) What is essential? (\textbf{experiencia previa}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
